Sanjeev Kumar, his son, opens and closes the shop

law_refs.quote: on or after the 9th day of June, 1952

tests.objects: Shyam Singh as tenant; Sanjeev Kumar as named son and alleged recipient; respondent no. 2 as purported recipient; tenanted printing shop.
tests.opposition: Shyam Singh denied a subletting or parting arrangement and characterized the son's activities as family assistance. This disputes the legal nature of the arrangement rather than providing a competing pre-1952 date.

opposition_refs.quote: Submission with regard to the subletting or parting with said shop with the Sanjeev Kumar has been declined by the Shyam Singh.
his son used to help him in his work due to his illness.

tests.rationale: The petitioner expressly places the alleged disposition after the statutory cutoff, and the described arrangement is documented in proceedings involving a 2008 notice. This supports the temporal placement of the disputed arrangement without establishing that the son's activities constituted a legal disposition. The exact transfer date remains unspecified.

source_refs.quote: Respondent no. 2 is a legal tenant and is in exclusive possession and in full control of the tenanted shop
he is running the business in the said shop himself exclusively and opens and closes the shop himself.

law_refs.quote: In subletting there exists the relationship of landlord and tenant as between the tenant and his sub-tenant and all the incidents of letting or tenancy have to be found, namely the transfer of an interest in the estate payment of rent, and the right to possession as against the tenant in respect of the Premises sublet.

tests.objects: Alleged subtenancy from Shyam Singh to respondent no. 2, apparently identified with his son Sanjeev Kumar, concerning the printing shop; equivalence of the two recipient descriptions is suggested but not expressly established in a single supplied statement.
tests.opposition: The written statement characterizes respondent no. 2 as the tenant's son assisting the family business. Shyam Singh and Sanjeev Kumar deny an independent business relationship of the kind alleged. The landlord also acknowledged continued printing activity and the existing business sign.

opposition_refs.quote: Respondent no. 2 is the son of respondent no. 1, who is only assisting the respondent no. 1 for conducting the business activities.
Sanjeev Kumar is neither partner nor the CASE No. RC - 01/08 4/10 employee in the said shop.
the board of S.R. Printer is still there.
He is only assisting his father.

tests.gap_reason: The supplied evidence does not establish a subtenancy agreement, rent paid by the son to Shyam Singh, transfer of an interest in the premises, or an independent right to possession against Shyam Singh. The recipient's identity across the respondent-number and named-son references also requires careful verification.
tests.rationale: The landlord's characterization of respondent no. 2 as a tenant and exclusive controller conflicts with evidence describing family assistance. Opening and closing the shop does not independently establish all incidents of a tenancy. The material is insufficient for a conclusive positive or negative assessment of the composite test.

source_refs.quote: has sublet, assigned and part with the tenanted shop with respondent no. 2 and has shifted himself in Bahadrabad, Distt. Haridwar, Uttrakhand.
has shifted himself Bahadrabad, Distt. Haridwar, Uttrakhand permanently.

law_refs.quote: In assignment the tenant has to divest himself of all the rights that he has as a tenant.

tests.objects: Shyam Singh's tenancy rights in the printing shop; alleged assignment to respondent no. 2 or Sanjeev Kumar.
tests.opposition: Shyam Singh expressly asserted continued control over the premises and business. His testimony describes Sanjeev Kumar as a son helping with operations rather than a person to whom tenancy rights were assigned.

opposition_refs.quote: Respondent no. 1 is in full control of his business as well as tenanted premises.
Submission with regard to the subletting or parting with said shop with the Sanjeev Kumar has been declined by the Shyam Singh.

tests.gap_reason: No instrument, admitted transaction, or prior finding establishes that Shyam Singh divested himself of all tenancy rights. The alleged permanent relocation and the respondent's competing control claim are unresolved.
tests.rationale: The petitioner alleges assignment and relocation. The tenant claims to retain control. Residence elsewhere, even if established, would not alone demonstrate assignment of all tenancy rights under the supplied test.

at present son of respondent no. 1 is carrying on the business

law_refs.quote: "parting with possession" must have been by the tenant.
The divestment or abandonment of the right to possession is necessary in order to invoke the clause of parting with possession

tests.objects: Shyam Singh as original tenant and alleged transferor; Sanjeev Kumar or respondent no. 2 as alleged recipient; entire tenanted shop.
tests.opposition: Shyam Singh claimed continued full control and described the son's work as assistance prompted by illness. Sanjeev Kumar corroborated the assistance account. Continued printing work and the existing business sign provide additional context against inferring a complete transfer from daily operation alone.

opposition_refs.quote: Respondent no. 1 is in full control of his business as well as tenanted premises.
his son used to help him in his work due to his illness.
He is only assisting his father.
tenanted premises is still being used for printing work, till today since the inception of tenancy.

tests.gap_reason: The material does not establish whether the tenant retained an enforceable right to possession, whether the son's operational control was exclusive in the legal sense, or whether Shyam Singh caused a divestment of both physical possession and the right to possession.
tests.rationale: The landlord's account supports the possibility of exclusive possession by the son. The opposing testimony supports continued parental control and assistance. Physical management of the shop does not by itself resolve the required legal-possession inquiry.

without the consent of the petitioner, who is landlord

law_refs.quote: without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord;

tests.objects: Petitioner landlord; tenant Shyam Singh; alleged recipient respondent no. 2 or Sanjeev Kumar; tenanted shop.
tests.opposition: The tenant denies any illegal subletting and maintains that the son merely assists in the business. No affirmative written-consent document appears in the supplied evidence.

opposition_refs.quote: respondent no. 1 has not illegally subleted the shop to respondent no. 2.
Respondent no. 2 is the son of respondent no. 1, who is only assisting the respondent no. 1 for conducting the business activities.

tests.gap_reason: The landlord alleges absence of written consent, but the sources contain no independent finding, written-consent record, or comprehensive evidence determining consent for the particular alleged disposition.
tests.rationale: The petitioner's assertion concerns the correct landlord, tenant, and alleged shop disposition. It is nevertheless an allegation, and the supplied record does not independently resolve the negative written-consent proposition.

law_refs.quote: So long as the lessee retains the legal possession of the whole of the premises he does not commit a breach of law against parting with the possession by allowing other people to use the same.
The mere user by other persons is no parting with Possession so long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself

tests.objects: Shyam Singh's alleged retained legal possession of the printing shop during use and operation by his son Sanjeev Kumar.
tests.opposition: The petitioner asserts that respondent no. 2 is in exclusive possession and full control, conducts the business independently, and opens and closes the shop. The petitioner also alleges that Shyam Singh permanently moved away.

opposition_refs.quote: Respondent no. 2 is in exclusive possession and in full control in the tenanted shop
has shifted himself Bahadrabad, Distt. Haridwar, Uttrakhand permanently.

tests.gap_reason: The conflicting testimony and allegations do not determine whether Shyam Singh continued to possess a legal right of possession or whether the son obtained a right that wholly ousted him. No supplied prior court finding resolves that conflict.
tests.rationale: The family-assistance account supports retained possession, while the exclusive-control allegation contests it. Neither is an established finding of legal entitlement. The negative-polarity retained-possession proposition therefore remains unresolved.

tests.objects: The tenanted printing shop operated as S.R. Printer; alleged disposition to respondent no. 2 or Sanjeev Kumar.
tests.opposition: The respondents dispute the characterization of the son's occupation and business activity as a disposition, but the materials do not identify a different property as the subject of that dispute.

opposition_refs.quote: respondent no. 1 has not illegally subleted the shop to respondent no. 2.

tests.rationale: The pleaded transaction, alleged occupation, and competing explanations consistently concern the same tenanted shop. This supports the premises-scope proposition without resolving subletting, assignment, or parting with possession.
